stimuli.title: Free to All: The Rise of the American Public Library
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] Today, anyone with a library card can walk into a public library and borrow a book, use a computer, or attend a class without paying a cent. It is easy to assume that libraries have always worked this way. In fact, the idea that a community should share its books freely, and pay for them together through taxes, took more than a century to win acceptance in the United States.

[2] In colonial America, books were expensive, and most were imported from Europe. A family might own a Bible, an almanac, and little else. In 1731, Benjamin Franklin and a group of friends in Philadelphia found a solution: they pooled their money to buy books that all of them could borrow. Their Library Company of Philadelphia was a subscription library. Members paid a fee to join and yearly dues after that, and only members could take books home. Similar libraries soon appeared in other towns. They spread reading, but only among people who could afford the price of membership.

[3] The next step came in 1833, when the small town of Peterborough, New Hampshire, voted to use public money to buy books that any resident could borrow free of charge. Peterborough's collection was modest, but the principle behind it was bold. Fifteen years later, Massachusetts lawmakers allowed the city of Boston to create a library paid for by taxpayers. When the Boston Public Library opened its doors in 1854, its supporters argued that a democracy depends on citizens who can inform themselves, and that a working person should have the same access to knowledge as a wealthy one. Decades later, the words “Free to All” were carved above the entrance of the library's grand new building.

[4] Still, most towns lacked the money to build libraries of their own. That changed when the steel industrialist Andrew Carnegie began giving away much of his enormous fortune. As a poor teenager in Pennsylvania, Carnegie had borrowed books from a local man who opened his private collection to working boys on Saturdays. Carnegie never forgot it. Between the 1880s and 1919, he paid for more than 1,600 library buildings across the United States. His gifts came with conditions, however. A town had to provide the land and promise to spend public money every year to buy books, pay staff, and keep the doors open. Carnegie believed that a community would value a library more if it shared the cost.

[5] Not everyone, though, was welcome in the libraries that resulted. In much of the South, Black residents were barred from public libraries or sent to small, poorly stocked branches. In 1939, five young Black men in Alexandria, Virginia, quietly entered the city's whites-only library, took books from the shelves, and sat down to read. They were arrested, but their protest drew attention to a basic contradiction: a library described as public was closed to part of the public. Decades of further struggle passed before libraries across the country opened their doors to all.

[6] Today's libraries look very different from Franklin's shelves of imported volumes. Patrons check out e-books, print job applications, and attend classes on everything from citizenship to computer coding. Yet the core idea has not changed since Peterborough's town meeting. A public library rests on a simple bargain: by paying a small share together, a community gives every member, rich or poor, a door to knowledge that no one could easily open alone.

stimuli.title: The Repair
stimuli.source: Original fiction written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] The bicycle had been leaning against the back of the garage for three summers, its tires gone soft as old fruit. Nadia wheeled it into the driveway on the first warm Saturday of April and called through the screen door, “Grandpa, you said you'd show me.”

[2] Emilio Reyes had said many things over the winter, most of them from his recliner. For thirty-one years he had kept the city's buses running, and in all that time, he liked to say, no engine had ever beaten him. He came outside slowly, one hand on the railing, and lowered himself onto the overturned bucket Nadia had set out for him.

[3] “Chain first,” he said. “Then brakes. Tires last. A rider can push a bike with a flat tire. She cannot stop one with bad brakes.”

[4] He reached for the wrench. His fingers closed around it, and for a moment the old certainty was there, the weight of the tool settling into his palm like a handshake between friends. Then the tremor began. It started in his thumb, the way it had for months now, and spread until the wrench chattered against the bolt like teeth in the cold. He set it down on the pavement very carefully, as if it might break.

[5] Nadia looked at the wrench and then at the maple tree, where nothing in particular was happening. “My hands are cleaner anyway,” she said. “Mom will yell if you get grease on your good shirt.”

[6] Emilio let out a breath that was almost a laugh. “Your mother has yelled about my shirts since she was nine years old.” He nodded at the wrench. “All right. Pick it up. No, not like a hammer. Like you're holding a pencil you mean to write with. Good. Now, a quarter turn to the left. Feel how it gives? That's the bolt telling you it's ready.”

[7] The morning went on like that. Emilio talked and Nadia worked. Twice she stripped a screw, and twice he told her about the year a brand-new mechanic had flooded an entire bus engine with oil, and how that mechanic had later become the best one in the yard. Nadia did not ask who the mechanic was. She suspected she knew.

[8] By noon the chain was clean and the brakes squeezed tight against the rims. Nadia pumped the tires until they were hard as apples, then swung a leg over the seat and rolled to the end of the driveway and back.

[9] “It pulls a little to the right,” she reported.

[10] “Then we're not finished,” Emilio said. He leaned forward on the bucket, his eyes bright, his hands folded quietly in his lap. “Bring it here. Tell me what you see.”

stimuli.title: Draft Memo: Summer Heat Safety Procedures
stimuli.source: Original document written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
The following memo is a first draft. Numbered blanks mark places that need editing. Answer the questions that follow.

MEMORANDUM
To: All Grounds and Landscaping Crews
From: Marcus Bell, Safety Coordinator
Date: May 28
Subject: Summer Heat Safety Procedures

Last summer, two members of our field crews were treated for heat exhaustion while mowing at Lakeview Park, (1) has almost no shade. Both workers recovered fully, but the incidents showed that our old procedures were not enough. Beginning June 1, the following rules will (2) every employee who works outdoors.

Water and shade must be available at every job site. Neither the crew leader nor the crew members (3) allowed to skip scheduled breaks when the temperature is above 90 degrees. Workers should drink about one cup of water every 15 to 20 (4) is a late warning sign of dehydration.

Crew leaders will check the heat index each morning, (5), and move workers to a shaded area if anyone shows signs of illness. The company has also updated (6) heat-illness training, which all crew members must complete by June 15.

Know the warning signs of heat illness, and act on them. (7) Heat illness can become life-threatening within minutes. (8), any worker who stops sweating, becomes confused, or collapses must be treated as a medical emergency, and someone must call 911 right away.

Thank you for looking out for yourselves and one another this summer. Please direct any questions to me at extension 214.

stimuli.title: A Four-Day Week Is Good for Workers and Residents
stimuli.source: By Andrea Collins, human resources director for the City of Riverton. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
Riverton is struggling to hire and keep the people who keep our city running. Last year, 14 percent of city employees left their jobs, and some positions, such as building inspector, stayed empty for more than six months. Moving most municipal employees to a four-day, 40-hour workweek (four ten-hour days instead of five eight-hour days) would help solve this problem while improving service to residents.

We do not have to guess how the change would work, because we have already tested it. For twelve months, the city's permit office and parks maintenance division, about 60 employees in all, worked four ten-hour days. The permit office stayed open from 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., Monday through Thursday, instead of 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday. Residents who work regular daytime jobs could finally visit before or after their own shifts. The average wait for a building permit fell from 18 business days to 12, and complaints about office hours dropped from 41 the year before to 9.

The pilot also helped employees. Sick days taken in the two departments fell by 22 percent compared with the year before. Job postings for those departments drew nearly twice as many applicants as similar postings elsewhere in city government. In an anonymous survey, 87 percent of pilot employees said they wanted to keep the schedule.

Taxpayers benefit too. Because many city buildings would close on Fridays, the city's facilities manager estimates that Riverton could save about $140,000 a year on electricity, heating, and cleaning. And employees who commute one fewer day each week spend less on gas and add less traffic to our roads.

Critics worry that residents will lose access to services on Fridays. But during the pilot, the permit office was open 44 hours a week, only one hour fewer than before, and its new early and late hours were the ones working residents could actually use. Emergency services such as police, fire, and water repair would keep their current around-the-clock schedules.

No schedule is perfect, and the city should keep measuring results as the change expands. But the evidence from our own pilot is clear. A four-day workweek would help Riverton attract workers, serve residents at more convenient times, and save money. The city council should approve it.

stimuli.title: Riverton Residents Need a Five-Day City Hall
stimuli.source: By Gary Pruitt, owner of Pruitt Plumbing and Heating. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
City Hall exists to serve the people who pay for it. A proposal to move most Riverton employees to a four-day workweek would put the convenience of city workers ahead of the needs of residents and businesses, and the council should reject it.

Start with the obvious problem: Friday. Under the plan, City Hall and most city offices would close every Friday. For a small business like mine, that is a real cost. When my crews need an inspection to finish a job, a three-day weekend for inspectors means a three-day delay for my customers. Contractors I talk to are worried about the same thing. Supporters point to a pilot program in the permit office, but that pilot covered only two departments and about 60 employees out of more than 900 on the city payroll. Results from a small, hand-picked group tell us little about how a citywide change would work.

Ten-hour days also raise safety concerns. Road crews and maintenance workers do physical, sometimes dangerous work. Research on long shifts in other industries has linked fatigue late in a shift to more mistakes and injuries. Asking a tired employee to operate heavy equipment in the tenth hour of a summer workday is asking for trouble.

Then there is cost. Police, fire, and water departments cannot close on Fridays, so they would stay on their current schedules. That means the city would be running two different systems, with two sets of rules for scheduling, overtime, and holidays. Managing that complexity will not be free.

I also worry about where this leads. If we give city workers a four-day week today, they will ask for a three-day week tomorrow, and taxpayers will be stuck with the bill. My neighbor, a retired teacher, told me she has never once been able to get anyone on the phone at City Hall. Imagine how much worse it will be with one fewer day.

Riverton's employees work hard, and many of them deserve better pay and better working conditions. But the city's first duty is to the public. Keep City Hall open five days a week.

stimuli.title: Trouble in the Hive
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep. The beekeepers' association in the table is fictional.
stimuli.html:
[1] Every February, a remarkable migration takes place on American highways. Trucks carrying stacked wooden boxes roll into California's Central Valley from as far away as Florida and Maine. Inside the boxes are honeybees, well over a million colonies of them, brought in to pollinate the almond orchards that bloom there each spring. Without the bees, the trees would produce few nuts. The almond harvest is an extreme example of a broader truth: many of the fruits, nuts, and vegetables people eat depend on bees to carry pollen from flower to flower.

[2] That is why beekeepers and scientists grew alarmed in the winter of 2006–2007, when some commercial beekeepers opened their hives to find them nearly empty. The worker bees had vanished, leaving behind the queen, a few young bees, and stores of honey. Researchers named the mystery colony collapse disorder. Reports of sudden collapses have since become less common, but the scare drew attention to a wider problem. Surveys of American beekeepers have repeatedly found that they lose a large share of their colonies each year, often 30 percent or more, far higher than the losses beekeepers once considered normal.

[3] Scientists now believe there is no single cause. The most serious threat may be the varroa mite, a parasite about the size of a pinhead that feeds on bees and spreads deadly viruses through a colony. The mite reached the United States in the 1980s and is now found in nearly every hive. Pesticides add to the danger. Some chemicals kill bees outright, while others, including a class of insecticides called neonicotinoids, may weaken bees' ability to find their way home. Poor nutrition plays a role as well. A honeybee colony needs pollen from many kinds of plants, but where a single crop stretches for miles, or where wildflowers have been cleared for development, bees may find little variety to eat. Finally, the long truck journeys themselves stress colonies that are already struggling.

[4] Surprisingly, the number of managed honeybee colonies in the United States has not dropped sharply in recent decades. The reason is that beekeepers work hard to replace what they lose. They divide strong colonies into two, buy new queens, and treat hives for mites. This constant rebuilding keeps the total number of colonies fairly steady, but it is expensive, and the rising costs are passed along to farmers who rent the bees and, eventually, to shoppers.

[5] The table below shows winter losses reported by members of the Three Rivers Beekeepers Association, a regional group, over four years.

WinterColonies in fallColonies lost by springPercent lost
2020–211,20038432%
2021–221,25045036%
2022–231,30035127%
2023–241,28044835%

[6] Some solutions are within reach. Farmers can plant strips of wildflowers along field edges, giving bees a more varied diet. Homeowners can replace part of a lawn with flowering native plants and avoid spraying insecticides while plants are in bloom. Researchers are breeding bees that groom mites off one another. None of these steps alone will solve the problem. Together, however, they may help ensure that the trucks keep rolling each February, and that the bees inside them survive the trip.

stimuli.title: The Bees We Overlook
stimuli.source: A letter to the editor. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
To the Editor:

[1] Your recent coverage of honeybee losses was welcome, but as a beekeeper for twenty-two years, I believe it told only half the story. The honeybee is not native to North America. European colonists brought it here in the 1600s, and today it is raised, fed, medicated, and moved around the country by its keepers much like any other farm animal. When I lose hives over the winter, as I do most years, I split my strongest colonies in the spring and order new queens by mail. By June, my bee yard is full again. My losses cost me time and money, and I take them seriously. But the honeybee itself is in no danger of disappearing.

[2] The same cannot be said for the roughly 4,000 species of bees that are native to this continent. Most of them live alone rather than in hives, and many nest in bare ground or hollow stems. No one splits their colonies or ships them replacement queens. When their habitat is plowed or paved, they simply vanish. In 2017, the rusty patched bumble bee became the first bee in the continental United States to be listed as endangered. Researchers believe that many other native species have declined as well, but because so few scientists study them, we do not know how many.

[3] Native bees matter. Bumble bees pollinate tomatoes and blueberries more effectively than honeybees do, and wild bees of many kinds help pollinate apple orchards and pumpkin fields at no charge to farmers. Some studies even suggest that large numbers of honeybees can compete with native bees for the same flowers.

[4] I am not asking anyone to stop keeping honeybees. I am asking readers to think beyond them. Leave a corner of your yard unmowed. Leave dead stems standing through the winter. Plant native flowers. The honeybee has thousands of keepers looking after it. Our native bees have only us.

— Ruth Halvorsen, beekeeper

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Andrew Carnegie created the idea of the free public library in the United States.
Subscription libraries were more successful than tax-supported libraries because members valued books they paid for.
The American public library grew slowly from private, fee-based collections into a service shared by whole communities, although access was not always equal.
Modern libraries have abandoned their original purpose in favor of offering technology and classes.
items.explain:
The passage traces a long development: fee-based subscription libraries (paragraph 2), the first tax-supported libraries in Peterborough and Boston (paragraph 3), Carnegie's buildings (paragraph 4), the exclusion of Black residents (paragraph 5), and today's libraries, which still rest on the same “simple bargain” (paragraph 6).

Carnegie did not create the idea; Peterborough and Boston had free libraries decades before his gifts. The passage never says subscription libraries were more successful, and paragraph 6 says the core idea “has not changed,” so libraries have not abandoned their purpose.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 3.

“Peterborough's collection was modest, but the principle behind it was bold.”

As used in the sentence, what does modest mean?
options: small or limited in size
shy and quiet in manner
free of charge to borrow
carefully chosen
items.explain:
The sentence contrasts the collection with the “bold” principle behind it: the collection itself was not impressive, but the idea was. In this context, modest means small or limited in size.

“Shy and quiet” describes a person, not a collection of books. The books were free to borrow, but that is stated elsewhere and is not what “modest” means. Nothing in the sentence says the books were carefully chosen.

items.prompt: Paragraph 4 is shown below. Click the sentence that best explains why Carnegie required towns to help pay for their libraries.
spans: Still, most towns lacked the money to build libraries of their own.
That changed when the steel industrialist Andrew Carnegie began giving away much of his enormous fortune.
As a poor teenager in Pennsylvania, Carnegie had borrowed books from a local man who opened his private collection to working boys on Saturdays.
Between the 1880s and 1919, he paid for more than 1,600 library buildings across the United States.
His gifts came with conditions, however.
A town had to provide the land and promise to spend public money every year to buy books, pay staff, and keep the doors open.
Carnegie believed that a community would value a library more if it shared the cost.
items.explain:
The last sentence gives Carnegie's reason: he “believed that a community would value a library more if it shared the cost.”

The sentence beginning “A town had to provide the land” describes what the conditions were, not why Carnegie set them.

items.prompt: Based on paragraph 4, what can be inferred about Carnegie's decision to pay for library buildings?
options: He wanted every library to be named after him.
His own experience borrowing books as a young worker helped convince him that libraries were valuable.
He believed that only wealthy people should be in charge of libraries.
He was required by law to give away most of his fortune.
items.explain:
The passage says that as a poor teenager Carnegie borrowed books from a man who opened his collection to working boys, and that “Carnegie never forgot it.” Placing this memory right before his library gifts suggests that the experience shaped his decision.

The passage never mentions naming libraries after him or any legal requirement. His rule that towns share the cost shows he wanted communities, not just the wealthy, to be responsible for libraries.

items.prompt: How is the passage mainly organized?
options: It describes a problem and then argues for one solution.
It compares two libraries point by point.
It lists the reasons for libraries from least to most important.
It traces how libraries changed over time, from the colonial era to today.
items.explain:
The passage moves in time order: 1731 (paragraph 2), 1833 and 1854 (paragraph 3), the 1880s to 1919 (paragraph 4), 1939 (paragraph 5), and “today” (paragraph 6). That is a chronological structure.

Although the passage mentions several libraries, it does not compare two of them point by point, and it does not argue for one solution or rank reasons by importance.

items.prompt: Using “Free to All,” arrange these milestones in American library history from earliest to latest. Drag each milestone into the correct position.
choices: The Boston Public Library opens to the public.
Benjamin Franklin and his friends found the Library Company of Philadelphia.
Five young men stage a sit-in at the Alexandria library.
Peterborough, New Hampshire, votes to buy books for free public use.
Andrew Carnegie pays for more than 1,600 library buildings.
items.explain: (1) Library Company of Philadelphia, 1731. (2) Peterborough's vote, 1833. (3) Boston Public Library opens, 1854. (4) Carnegie's gifts, from the 1880s to 1919. (5) The Alexandria sit-in, 1939.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 5?
options: to argue that the federal government should run all public libraries
to explain why Carnegie's conditions failed in Southern towns
to show that the promise of a library “free to all” was not fully kept for many years
to suggest that subscription libraries were fairer than public libraries
items.explain:
Paragraph 5 begins, “Not everyone, though, was welcome,” and describes how Black residents were barred from libraries. It names the “basic contradiction” that a library “described as public was closed to part of the public.” This shows the ideal of “Free to All” from paragraph 3 was not yet a reality.

The paragraph does not discuss the federal government, does not say Carnegie's conditions failed, and does not praise subscription libraries.

items.prompt: Which details from the passage support the idea that public libraries were meant to serve people regardless of how much money they had? Select two answers.
options: Boston's supporters argued that a working person should have the same access to knowledge as a wealthy one.
Members of the Library Company paid a fee to join and yearly dues after that.
Most books in colonial America were imported from Europe.
Peterborough voted to buy books that any resident could borrow free of charge.
Carnegie required each town to provide the land for its library.
A colonial family might own a Bible, an almanac, and little else.
items.explain:
Boston's argument that a working person deserves “the same access to knowledge as a wealthy one” and Peterborough's books that “any resident could borrow free of charge” both show libraries designed for everyone, rich or poor.

The Library Company's fees show the opposite, a library limited to those who could pay. Imported books, the land requirement, and the family's few books are true details but do not show service regardless of wealth.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, why does Nadia most likely look at the maple tree, “where nothing in particular was happening”?
options: She is bored and wants the repair to end quickly.
She wants to avoid embarrassing her grandfather by staring at his shaking hands.
She has noticed a problem with the tree that worries her.
She is angry that her grandfather broke his promise to help her.
items.explain:
Nadia looks away right after Emilio's tremor forces him to set down the wrench. Since “nothing in particular was happening” at the tree, she is not looking at it for its own sake; she is giving her grandfather privacy. Her next line, a light excuse about clean hands and grease, also spares his pride.

Nothing suggests she is bored or angry; she stays all morning and works hard. The narrator says nothing was happening at the tree, which rules out a problem there.

items.prompt: In paragraph 4, the author writes that the wrench “chattered against the bolt like teeth in the cold.” What is the main effect of this comparison?
options: It emphasizes how noticeable and uncontrollable Emilio's tremor is.
It shows that the morning is colder than Nadia expected.
It suggests that the bolt is too rusty to move.
It shows that Emilio is angry at Nadia.
items.explain:
Chattering teeth shake and rattle on their own, beyond a person's control. Comparing the wrench to them shows that Emilio's tremor is strong enough to be heard and cannot be stopped.

The comparison is figurative; the story says it is “the first warm Saturday,” so it is not about cold weather. The bolt later turns easily for Nadia, and nothing shows anger.

items.prompt: In paragraph 4, the weight of the wrench settles into Emilio's palm “like a handshake between friends.” This description suggests that Emilio
options: has just met Nadia for the first time.
prefers working with tools to talking with people.
is nervous about using a wrench again.
has long felt comfortable and confident using tools.
items.explain:
A handshake between friends is familiar and easy. The sentence also says “for a moment the old certainty was there.” Together these show that holding a tool has long felt natural and confident to Emilio.

Nadia is his granddaughter, so they are not meeting for the first time. The simile is about familiarity, not a preference for tools over people, and “old certainty” is the opposite of nervousness.

items.prompt: Paragraph 7 is shown below. Click the sentence that suggests the mechanic in Emilio's story was Emilio himself.
spans: The morning went on like that.
Twice she stripped a screw, and twice he told her about the year a brand-new mechanic had flooded an entire bus engine with oil, and how that mechanic had later become the best one in the yard.
Nadia did not ask who the mechanic was.
items.explain:
“She suspected she knew” hints that Nadia has figured out who the mechanic was. Since paragraph 2 says Emilio kept the city's buses running for thirty-one years and “no engine had ever beaten him,” the best mechanic in the yard was most likely Emilio.

The sentence before it says only that Nadia did not ask; it does not suggest an answer.

items.prompt: Why does Emilio tell Nadia the story about the brand-new mechanic?
options: to warn her that she is not suited to mechanical work
to boast that he was once the best mechanic in the yard
to encourage her by showing that early mistakes do not prevent later success
to distract her from noticing his shaking hands
items.explain:
Emilio tells the story each time Nadia strips a screw (“Twice she stripped a screw, and twice he told her”). The story's point is that a beginner who made a big mistake “later became the best one in the yard,” which reassures Nadia after her own mistakes.

He keeps teaching her, so he is not warning her off. He never names himself, so the story is not a boast. It is timed to her mistakes, not to his tremor.

items.prompt: Which details show that Emilio is still a knowledgeable mechanic even though he can no longer do the work himself? Select two answers.
options: He comes outside slowly, with one hand on the railing.
He explains that the chain comes first, then the brakes, then the tires, and gives a reason for that order.
He sits on an overturned bucket while Nadia works.
His fingers begin to tremble on the wrench.
He shows Nadia how to hold the wrench and how to feel when a bolt is ready to turn.
He jokes that Nadia's mother has complained about his shirts for years.
items.explain:
Emilio's repair order, with the reason that “a rider can push a bike with a flat tire” but cannot stop one with bad brakes (paragraph 3), and his precise instructions about the grip and the “quarter turn” (paragraph 6) both show expert knowledge.

Walking slowly, sitting on the bucket, and the tremor show his physical limits, not his knowledge. The joke about shirts shows his humor and family history.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 2.

“Emilio Reyes had said many things over the winter, most of them from his recliner.”

Together with paragraph 1, this sentence suggests that Emilio
options: had been too busy at work to help Nadia during the winter.
had been inactive for months and had made promises he had not yet kept.
enjoyed telling stories more than fixing things.
had refused to help Nadia with the bicycle.
items.explain:
In paragraph 1 Nadia reminds him, “you said you'd show me,” and the bike has sat untouched for three summers. Saying “many things” from a recliner suggests talk without action and a winter spent sitting. So Emilio had been inactive and had not yet kept his promise.

He is retired after thirty-one years, so he was not busy at work. He never refused; he comes outside as soon as she asks. The sentence is about inactivity, not a preference for storytelling.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
options: Skill and pride can be passed on to others even when a person's physical abilities fade.
Young people learn best when adults leave them to solve problems alone.
Old machines are rarely worth the effort it takes to repair them.
Families should never keep secrets about a person's health.
items.explain:
Emilio can no longer hold the wrench steadily, but by guiding Nadia's hands he finds a new way to use his skill. By the end, with his “eyes bright,” he is eager to keep teaching (“Then we're not finished”). The story shows knowledge passing from one generation to the next.

Nadia does not work alone; Emilio guides every step. The repair succeeds, so the story does not suggest old machines are not worth fixing. No one in the story keeps a secret.

items.prompt: In the final paragraph, Emilio leans forward “his eyes bright, his hands folded quietly in his lap.” What does this description mainly suggest?
options: He is tired and ready to stop for the day.
He is disappointed that the bicycle still has a problem.
He plans to finish the repair himself after Nadia leaves.
He has found a satisfying new role as a teacher rather than the one doing the work.
items.explain:
Bright eyes and leaning forward show eagerness, while his folded hands show that he is no longer reaching for the tools. He says, “Tell me what you see,” inviting Nadia to diagnose the problem. He is content to guide rather than do.

“Then we're not finished” rules out being ready to stop, and his eagerness rules out disappointment. Nothing suggests he will take over the work, and his tremor would make that unlikely.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Last summer, two members of our field crews were treated for heat exhaustion while mowing at Lakeview Park, {{0}} has almost no shade.”

options: who
that
what
which

items.explain:
The clause adds extra information about a place (Lakeview Park) and is set off by a comma, so it needs which.

“Who” refers to people, not places. “That” is not used after a comma to begin a nonessential clause. “What” cannot introduce a clause describing a noun.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Beginning June 1, the following rules will {{0}} every employee who works outdoors.”

options: affect
effect
effects
affects

items.explain:
The sentence needs a verb meaning “to influence” after the helping verb “will,” so the correct choice is affect.

“Effect” is usually a noun meaning a result (as a verb it means “to bring about,” which does not fit). “Effects” and “affects” have an -s ending, which cannot follow “will.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Neither the crew leader nor the crew members {{0}} allowed to skip scheduled breaks when the temperature is above 90 degrees.”

options: is
are
was
has been

items.explain:
With neither … nor, the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. The closer subject is “crew members,” which is plural, so the verb is are. The rule applies now and going forward, so present tense is correct.

“Is” and “has been” are singular and would agree only with “crew leader.” “Was” is singular and past tense.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Workers should drink about one cup of water every 15 to 20 {{0}} is a late warning sign of dehydration.”

options: minutes, thirst
minutes thirst
minutes; thirst
minutes, however, thirst

items.explain:
The sentence joins two complete sentences: “Workers should drink … every 15 to 20 minutes” and “thirst is a late warning sign of dehydration.” A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses.

A comma alone creates a comma splice, and no punctuation creates a fused run-on. “However” is not a conjunction, so “, however,” still leaves a comma splice.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Crew leaders will check the heat index each morning, {{0}}, and move workers to a shaded area if anyone shows signs of illness.”

options: adjusting start times on hot days
they should adjust start times on hot days
adjust start times on hot days
start times will be adjusted on hot days

items.explain:
The sentence lists three actions crew leaders will take: check the heat index, ___, and move workers. Items in a series must have the same form, so the middle item also needs a base verb: adjust start times on hot days.

“Adjusting” is an -ing form, and the other two choices add a new subject, which breaks the parallel pattern.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The company has also updated {{0}} heat-illness training, which all crew members must complete by June 15.”

options: it's
their
its
its'

items.explain:
The training belongs to the company, which is a singular noun, so the singular possessive pronoun its is correct.

“It's” means “it is.” “Their” is plural and does not agree with “company.” “Its'” is not a word.

items.prompt:
Choose the sentence that should fill blank (7) in the memo, just before “Heat illness can become life-threatening within minutes.”

{{0}}

options: If you feel dizzy or confused, stop working and tell your crew leader immediately.
Feeling dizzy or confused, your crew leader must be told immediately.
Feeling dizzy or confused, work must stop and be reported immediately.
Feeling dizzy or confused, the shade should be found right away.

items.explain:
The sentence beginning “If you feel dizzy or confused” is clear and correct: the person who feels dizzy (“you”) is the one told to stop working and tell the crew leader.

The other three begin with “Feeling dizzy or confused,” which must describe the subject that comes right after the comma. In those sentences the subject is “your crew leader,” “work,” or “the shade,” none of which can feel dizzy. These are dangling modifiers.

items.prompt:
Read these sentences from the memo. Choose the option that correctly completes the second sentence.

“Heat illness can become life-threatening within minutes. {{0}}, any worker who stops sweating, becomes confused, or collapses must be treated as a medical emergency, and someone must call 911 right away.”

options: However
For example
Instead
For this reason

items.explain:
The first sentence gives a reason (heat illness becomes dangerous quickly), and the second gives the result (treat these signs as an emergency and call 911). A cause-and-effect transition is needed: For this reason.

“However” and “Instead” signal a contrast that is not there. The second sentence is a rule that follows from the first, not an example of it, so “For example” does not fit.

essay.prompt:
The articles present arguments from a supporter and a critic of moving a city's municipal employees to a four-day workweek.

In your response, analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported. Use relevant and specific evidence from both articles to support your response.

Type your response in the box. This task may require approximately 45 minutes to complete.

items.prompt:
Read this line from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Dear Mr. Ortiz{{0}}”
items.explain:
In a formal business letter, the greeting ends with a colon: “Dear Mr. Ortiz:”.

A semicolon joins two independent clauses and is never used after a greeting. A period would end the greeting as if it were a sentence.

items.prompt:
Choose the option that correctly completes this sentence from Tamika Ross's letter.

“On March 4, Sweet Rise Bakery purchased a Model 600 proofing cabinet from your company, {{0}} sales representative assured us that the unit would be ready to use on delivery.”

options: who's
whose
who
whom

items.explain:
The sales representative belongs to the company, so the sentence needs the possessive whose.

“Who's” means “who is,” which makes no sense here (“who is sales representative”). “Who” and “whom” are not possessive.

items.prompt:
Choose the option that correctly completes this sentence from Tamika Ross's letter.

“Since ours was installed, however, its temperature has never climbed above 70 degrees{{0}} the dial is set to 95 degrees.”

options: . Even though
, even though
; even though
. Although

items.explain:
“Even though the dial is set to 95 degrees” is a dependent clause; it cannot stand alone. It must attach to the main clause, and a comma is correct: “…above 70 degrees, even though the dial is set to 95 degrees.”

Starting a new sentence with “Even though” or “Although” creates a fragment. A semicolon should join two independent clauses, not an independent clause and a dependent one.

items.prompt:
Choose the option that correctly completes this sentence from Tamika Ross's letter.

“On September 22, a technician from your company met with my business partner and {{0}} at the bakery.”

options: myself
I
me
mine

items.explain:
The pronoun is the object of the preposition “with,” so it must be in the object case: me. A quick test is to remove “my business partner and”: “met with me,” not “met with I.”

“Myself” is reflexive and is used only when the subject of the sentence is also “I.” “Mine” is possessive.

items.prompt:
Choose the option that correctly completes this sentence from Tamika Ross's letter.

“The results of his inspection {{0}} clear: the cabinet's heating element is defective and must be replaced.”

options: is
has been
was being
are

items.explain:
The subject is results, which is plural. “Of his inspection” is a prepositional phrase and does not change the subject. A plural subject takes the plural verb are.

“Is,” “has been,” and “was being” are singular forms that wrongly agree with “inspection.”

items.prompt:
Read these sentences from the letter. Choose the option that correctly completes the second sentence.

“Without a working cabinet, our dough rises slowly and unevenly. {{0}}, we have had to turn down two large wholesale orders this month.”

options: As a result
Nevertheless
Similarly
On the other hand

items.explain:
Turning down orders is a consequence of the dough rising poorly, so a cause-and-effect transition is needed: As a result.

“Nevertheless” and “On the other hand” signal contrast, and “Similarly” signals a comparison; none of those relationships fits.

items.prompt:
Choose the option that correctly completes this sentence from Tamika Ross's letter.

“Your one-year warranty covers defective parts, so the cabinet should {{0}} been repaired or replaced at no cost by now.”

options: of
had
have
has

items.explain:
After a helping verb such as “should,” the correct form is have plus a past participle: “should have been repaired.”

“Should of” is a common error that comes from the way “should've” sounds when spoken. “Had” and “has” cannot follow “should.”

items.prompt: Taken as a whole, what is “Trouble in the Hive” mainly about?
options: Colony collapse disorder remains the main reason honeybee colonies die each year.
Honeybee colonies face several combined threats, and although beekeepers replace their losses, the problem is costly and calls for a range of solutions.
Pesticides are the single cause of honeybee losses and should be banned.
The number of honeybee colonies in the United States has fallen sharply in recent decades.
items.explain:
The passage explains that bees are vital to farming (paragraph 1), that losses are high (paragraph 2), that “there is no single cause” (paragraph 3), that rebuilding keeps numbers steady but “is expensive” (paragraph 4), and that several steps together may help (paragraph 6).

Paragraph 2 says sudden collapses “have since become less common.” Paragraph 3 lists pesticides as one cause among several. Paragraph 4 says colony numbers have not dropped sharply.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the table in “Trouble in the Hive”?
options: The association's winter losses went down steadily from 2020–21 to 2023–24.
The association had fewer colonies each fall than it had the fall before.
The association lost more than one-fourth of its colonies in every winter shown.
Varroa mites caused most of the association's winter losses.
items.explain:
One-fourth is 25 percent. The percent lost each winter was 32%, 36%, 27%, and 35%, all greater than 25%. (Check: 384 ÷ 1,200 = 0.32; 450 ÷ 1,250 = 0.36; 351 ÷ 1,300 = 0.27; 448 ÷ 1,280 = 0.35.)

Losses rose, fell, and rose again, so they did not go down steadily. Fall colony counts rose from 1,200 to 1,250 to 1,300 before dipping to 1,280. The table shows no causes of loss, so it cannot support a claim about mites.

items.prompt: Based on “Trouble in the Hive,” sort each item into the correct category. Drag each item into the correct box.
choices: Varroa mites feeding on bees and spreading viruses
Fields where a single crop stretches for miles
Breeding bees that groom mites off one another
Long truck journeys to distant orchards
Planting wildflower strips along field edges
bins: Effort to protect or rebuild colonies
items.explain:
Threats (paragraph 3): varroa mites, single-crop fields that leave bees “little variety to eat,” and long truck journeys that “stress colonies.”

Efforts: dividing colonies (paragraph 4), and breeding mite-grooming bees and planting wildflower strips (paragraph 6).

items.prompt: Why does the author begin paragraph 4 with the word “Surprisingly”?
options: to signal that the information that follows is the opposite of what readers might expect after reading about heavy losses
to show that the author does not believe the survey results in paragraph 2
to introduce a new cause of colony losses
to suggest that beekeepers have been hiding their losses from the public
items.explain:
Paragraphs 2 and 3 describe high yearly losses and many threats. Readers would expect the total number of colonies to be falling, so the author signals a contrast with “Surprisingly”: the number “has not dropped sharply.” The paragraph then explains why.

The author accepts the survey results, does not add a new cause in paragraph 4, and describes beekeepers' rebuilding openly, not secretly.

items.prompt: Based on paragraph 4, which statement would the author most likely agree with?
options: Because colony numbers are steady, honeybee losses are no longer a concern.
Farmers should stop renting honeybees to pollinate their crops.
Beekeepers exaggerate their losses so that they can charge farmers more.
Steady colony numbers can hide a serious problem, because they depend on costly replacement work.
items.explain:
The author says rebuilding “keeps the total number of colonies fairly steady, but it is expensive,” with costs passed on to farmers and shoppers. The word “but” shows that steady numbers do not mean the problem is solved.

The author never says losses are no longer a concern, never tells farmers to stop renting bees, and never accuses beekeepers of exaggerating.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 1?
options: to argue that almonds should no longer be grown in California
to show, through a vivid example, how heavily some farming depends on honeybees
to explain how beekeepers keep bees safe on long truck trips
to compare honeybees with animals that migrate on their own
items.explain:
Paragraph 1 opens with the striking image of trucks carrying over a million colonies to almond orchards, notes that the trees “would produce few nuts” without them, and calls this “an extreme example of a broader truth” about crops depending on bees.

The author does not oppose almond growing, does not explain how bees are kept safe (paragraph 3 says the trips actually stress colonies), and makes no comparison with other migrating animals.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the main claim of Halvorsen's letter?
options: Native bees deserve more public concern, because unlike honeybees, no one replaces their losses.
People should stop keeping honeybees in order to protect native bees.
Scientists have exaggerated honeybee losses for many years.
Native bees pollinate every crop better than honeybees do.
items.explain:
Halvorsen argues that honeybee losses are replaced by keepers (paragraph 1) while native bees “simply vanish” (paragraph 2), and she ends: “The honeybee has thousands of keepers looking after it. Our native bees have only us.”

She says directly, “I am not asking anyone to stop keeping honeybees.” She never says scientists exaggerated losses; she takes her own losses “seriously.” She says bumble bees pollinate tomatoes and blueberries better, not every crop.

items.prompt: Paragraph 2 of the letter is shown below. Click the sentence in which the writer admits a limit to what is known about native bees.
spans: The same cannot be said for the roughly 4,000 species of bees that are native to this continent.
Most of them live alone rather than in hives, and many nest in bare ground or hollow stems.
No one splits their colonies or ships them replacement queens.
When their habitat is plowed or paved, they simply vanish.
In 2017, the rusty patched bumble bee became the first bee in the continental United States to be listed as endangered.
Researchers believe that many other native species have declined as well, but because so few scientists study them, we do not know how many.
items.explain:
The last sentence admits uncertainty: “because so few scientists study them, we do not know how many” native species have declined.

The other sentences state facts or claims with confidence. The 2017 sentence gives a specific, known fact rather than a limit to knowledge.

items.prompt: Why does Halvorsen describe splitting her colonies and ordering new queens by mail in paragraph 1?
options: to show that beekeeping has become too expensive for most people
to explain how she first became interested in bees
to show that people can replace honeybee losses, unlike losses of native bees
to argue that queens bought by mail are healthier than other queens
items.explain:
Her example ends with “By June, my bee yard is full again” and “the honeybee itself is in no danger of disappearing.” Paragraph 2 then contrasts this: “No one splits their colonies or ships them replacement queens” for native bees. The detail sets up that contrast.

She mentions cost only briefly, says nothing about how she started keeping bees, and does not compare the health of different queens.

items.prompt: On which point do the author of “Trouble in the Hive” and Halvorsen agree?
options: Varroa mites are the greatest threat to all bees in North America.
Large numbers of honeybees compete with native bees for the same flowers.
Native bees could pollinate the almond orchards in place of honeybees.
Beekeepers are able to rebuild their colonies after losses.
items.explain:
“Trouble in the Hive” says beekeepers “divide strong colonies into two, buy new queens” to replace losses (paragraph 4). Halvorsen says she splits her colonies and orders new queens, and “by June, my bee yard is full again.” Both describe rebuilding after losses.

Only “Trouble in the Hive” discusses varroa mites, and it calls them a threat to honeybees, not to all bees. Only Halvorsen mentions competition between honeybees and native bees. Neither text says native bees could pollinate the almond orchards.

items.prompt: Which statements describe ways that Halvorsen's letter differs from “Trouble in the Hive”? Select two answers.
options: It explains how varroa mites spread viruses through a colony.
It focuses mainly on native bees rather than on honeybees.
It reports losses from a regional beekeepers' association.
It argues that the honeybee itself is in no danger of disappearing.
It mentions that honeybee colonies can be divided to replace losses.
items.explain:
Halvorsen's letter shifts the focus to native bees (paragraphs 2–4), while “Trouble in the Hive” is about honeybees. She also states that “the honeybee itself is in no danger of disappearing,” a claim the article never makes; the article treats honeybee losses as a serious, costly problem.

Varroa mites and the association's table appear only in “Trouble in the Hive,” not in the letter. Dividing colonies appears in both texts, so it is not a difference.

items.prompt: Based on her letter, Halvorsen would most likely say that “Trouble in the Hive”
options: leaves out the native bees whose losses no one replaces.
exaggerates the danger posed by varroa mites.
is wrong that the number of honeybee colonies has stayed steady.
should not have mentioned the costs passed along to farmers.
items.explain:
Halvorsen says the coverage of honeybee losses “told only half the story.” The missing half, in her view, is the native bees that “simply vanish” because no one replaces them. “Trouble in the Hive” discusses only honeybees.

She never mentions mites. She actually agrees that honeybee numbers are maintained (“my bee yard is full again”). She herself notes that losses cost “time and money,” so she would not object to discussing costs.

items.prompt: Compared with “Trouble in the Hive,” Halvorsen's letter is more
options: statistical, relying mainly on data tables to make its point.
personal, drawing on the writer's own experience to support an argument.
neutral, presenting several sides without taking a position.
technical, explaining in detail how pesticides affect bees.
items.explain:
Halvorsen writes in the first person about her “twenty-two years” as a beekeeper, her own winter losses, and her own bee yard, and she ends with direct requests to readers. That is a personal, argumentative approach.

Only “Trouble in the Hive” includes a data table and discusses pesticides. Halvorsen clearly takes a position, so the letter is not neutral.

items.prompt: Which sentence from the letter provides the most specific, verifiable evidence that native bees are in trouble?
options: “When their habitat is plowed or paved, they simply vanish.”
“Our native bees have only us.”
“Most of them live alone rather than in hives, and many nest in bare ground or hollow stems.”
“In 2017, the rusty patched bumble bee became the first bee in the continental United States to be listed as endangered.”
items.explain:
The 2017 endangered listing names a specific species, a specific year, and an official action that a reader could check. It directly shows that at least one native bee is in serious decline.

“They simply vanish” is a broad, general statement. “Our native bees have only us” is an emotional appeal, not evidence. The sentence about living alone and nesting in the ground describes how native bees live but does not show they are in trouble.
